'''Lewis's trilemma''' is an [[apologetic]] argument traditionally used to argue for the [[Incarnation (Christianity)|divinity of Jesus]] by postulating that the only alternatives are that he was evil or [[Mental health of Jesus|mad]].<ref name="Dock">Lewis, C. S. (1970). "Christian Apologetics", ''God in the Dock''. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans. pp. 100–101. From a paper read to an assembly of Anglican priests and youth leaders during Easter 1945.</ref> One version was popularised by [[University of Oxford]] literary scholar and writer [[C. S. Lewis]] in a [[BBC]] radio talk and in his writings. It is sometimes described as the "'''Lunatic, Liar, or Lord'''", or "'''Mad, Bad, or God'''" argument. It takes the form of a [[trilemma]]—a choice among three options, each of which is in some way difficult to accept.

A form of the argument can be found as early as 1846, and many other versions of the argument preceded Lewis's formulation in the 1940s. The argument has played an important part in [[Christian apologetics]]. Criticisms of the argument have included that it assumes that Jesus claimed to be God, while biblical scholars who wrote books about the [[historical Jesus]] agree that "Jesus did not spend his ministry declaring himself to be divine",<ref name="Hick page 27"/><ref name="p696"/> and that it is logically unsound since it presents an incomplete set of options.

==History==
This argument has been used in various forms throughout church history.<ref>{{cite web |last=Barton |first=Kyle |title=The History Of The Liar, Lunatic, Lord Trilemma |url=https://conversantfaith.com/2012/05/04/the-history-of-liar-lunatic-lord-trilemma/#ref2 |website=Conversant Faith |date=5 May 2012 |access-date=19 May 2019}}</ref> It was used by the American preacher [[Mark Hopkins (educator)|Mark Hopkins]] in ''Lectures on the Evidences of Christianity'' (1846), a book based on lectures delivered in 1844.<ref>Hopkins, Mark (1846). ''Lectures on the Evidences of Christianity''. Lecture VIII. "... either ... those claims were well-founded, or of a hopeless insanity. ... No impostor of common sense could have had the folly to prefer such claims."</ref> Another early use of this approach was by the Scottish preacher "Rabbi" [[John Duncan (theologian)|John Duncan]] (1796–1870), around 1859–1860. He stated:

<blockquote>"Christ either deceived mankind by conscious fraud, or He was Himself deluded and self-deceived, or He was Divine. There is no getting out of this trilemma. It is inexorable."<ref>Knight, William (1870). ''Colloquia Peripatetica''. p. 109. Knight explains that the conversations quoted took place during the summers of 1859 and 1860.</ref></blockquote>

[[J. Gresham Machen]] used a similar line of argument in fifth chapter of his famous work ''[[Christianity and Liberalism]]'' (1923). There, Machen says: 

<blockquote>"The real trouble is that the lofty claim of Jesus, if ... the claim was unjustified, places a moral stain upon Jesus' character. What shall be thought of a human being who lapsed so far from the path of humility and sanity as to believe the eternal destinies of the world were committed into his hands? The truth is that if Jesus be merely an example, he is not a worthy example for he claimed to be far more."<ref>{{cite book | last = Machen|first=J. Gresham|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WVBgg00gJLcC|chapter=Christ|title=Christianity and Liberalism|date=1923|publisher=Eerdmans|pages=80–116|isbn=978-0-8028-1121-9 }}</ref></blockquote>

Among others who used this approach were [[N. P. Williams]],<ref>Williams, N. P. (1923). [http://anglicanhistory.org/england/npwilliams/deity1923.html "The Deity of Christ"]. Transcribed by Kempton, Wayne (2013). ''The Congress Books: No. 4''. Retrieved 10 May 2024 – via Project Canterbury.</ref> [[R. A. Torrey]],<ref>{{cite web |last=Torrey |first=R. A. |date=n.d. |title=Some Reasons Why I Believe the Bible to Be the Word of God |url=http://www.wheaton.edu/bgc/archives/docs/torreysermon.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031211040248/https://www.wheaton.edu/bgc/archives/docs/torreysermon.html |archive-date=11 December 2003 |access-date=9 May 2024 |via=Billy Graham Center}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Torrey |first=Torrey |url=https://www.wholesomewords.org/etexts/torrey/deity2.html |title=The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith |publisher=George H. Doran |year=1918 |location=New York |access-date=9 May 2024 |via=Wholesome Words}}</ref> and [[W. E. Biederwolf]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Biederwolf|first=W. E.|year=1984|chapter=Yes, He Arose|editor-last=Hutson|editor-first=Curtis|title=Great Preaching on the Resurrection: Seventeen Messages|publisher=Sword of the Lord Publishers|page=29}}</ref> The writer [[G. K. Chesterton]] used something similar to the trilemma in his book, ''[[The Everlasting Man]]'' (1925),<ref>{{cite book|last1=Chesterton|first1=Gilbert Keith|title=The Everlasting Man|date=1993|publisher=Ignatius Press|location=San Francisco|pages=196–198}}</ref> which Lewis cited in 1962 as the second book that most influenced him.<ref>{{cite web|last=Zaleski|first=Carol|date=14 June 2011|title=C. S. Lewis's Aeneid|url=http://www.christiancentury.org/article/2011-05/c-s-lewis-s-aeneid|work=Christian Century|access-date=27 September 2014}}</ref>

==Lewis's formulation==
Lewis was an Oxford [[medieval literature]] scholar, popular writer, Christian apologist, and former [[atheist]]. He used the [[argument]] outlined below in a series of BBC radio talks later published as the book ''[[Mere Christianity]]''. There, he states:

<blockquote>"I am trying here to prevent anyone saying the really foolish thing that people often say about Him: I'm ready to accept Jesus as a great moral teacher, but I don't accept his claim to be God. That is the one thing we must not say. A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would either be a lunatic—on the level with the man who says he is a poached egg—or else he would be the Devil of Hell. You must make your choice. Either this man was, and is, the Son of God, or else a madman or something worse. You can shut him up for a fool, you can spit at him and kill him as a demon or you can fall at his feet and call him Lord and God, but let us not come with any patronizing nonsense about his being a great human teacher. He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to. ... Now it seems to me obvious that He was neither a lunatic nor a fiend: and consequently, however strange or terrifying or unlikely it may seem, I have to accept the view that He was and is God."<ref>Lewis, C. S. (1952). ''[[Mere Christianity]]''. New York: Macmillan. pp. 40–41. In all editions, this is Book II, Chapter 3, "The Shocking Alternative".</ref></blockquote>

Lewis, who had spoken extensively on Christianity to [[Royal Air Force]] personnel, was aware that many ordinary people did not believe Jesus was God but saw him rather as "a 'great human teacher' who was deified by his superstitious followers"; his argument is intended to overcome this.<ref name=Dock/> It is based on a traditional assumption that, in his words and deeds, Jesus was asserting a claim to be God. For example, in ''Mere Christianity'', Lewis refers to what he says are Jesus's claims:

*to have authority to forgive sins—behaving as if "He was the party chiefly concerned, the person chiefly offended in all offences"<ref name="auto">Lewis, C. S. (1952). ''Mere Christianity''. New York: Macmillan. p. 40.</ref>
*to have always existed; and
*to intend to come back to judge the world at the end of time.<ref name="auto"/>

Lewis implies that these amount to a claim to be God and argues that they logically exclude the possibility that Jesus was merely "a great moral teacher", because he believes no ordinary human making such claims could possibly be rationally or morally reliable. Elsewhere, he refers to this argument as "the {{Lang|la|aut Deus aut malus homo}}" ("either God or a bad man"),<ref>Lewis, C. S. (1945). ''God in the Dock: Essays on Theology and Ethics''. Eerdmans. p. 101. Letter to Owen Barfield, c. August 1939, printed in Hooper, Walter Hooper ed. (2004). ''The Collected Letters of C. S. Lewis, Volume 2''. Harper Collins. p. 269.</ref> a reference to an earlier version of the argument used by [[Henry Parry Liddon]] in his 1866 [[Bampton Lectures]], in which Liddon argued for the divinity of Jesus based on a number of grounds, including the claims he believed Jesus made.<ref>[[Henry Parry Liddon|Liddon, Henry Parry]] (1867). ''The Divinity of Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ''. Lecture IV. London. Liddon's version was "Christus si non Deus non bonus". According to [[Charles Gore]] (''The Incarnation of the Son of God'', 1890), Liddon could not recall the source of the epigram but Gore thought the argument went back to [[Victorinus Afer]]. Appendices, p. 238.</ref>

=== In Narnia ===
A version of this argument appears in Lewis's fantasy novel ''[[The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe]]''. When Lucy and Edmund return from Narnia (her second visit and his first), Edmund tells Peter and Susan that he was playing along with Lucy and pretending they went to Narnia. Peter and Susan believe Edmund and are worried that Lucy might be mentally ill, so they seek out the Professor whose house they are living in. After listening to them explain the situation and asking them some questions, he responds:

<blockquote>"{{'}}Logic!' said the Professor half to himself. 'Why don't they teach logic at these schools? There are only three possibilities. Either your sister is telling lies, or she is mad, or she is telling the truth. You know she doesn't tell lies and it is obvious she is not mad. For the moment then, and unless any further evidence turns up, we must assume she is telling the truth.{{'}}"<ref>Lewis, C. S. (1950). ''The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe''. HarperCollins.</ref></blockquote>

==Influence==
===Christian===
The trilemma has continued to be used in Christian apologetics since Lewis, notably by writers like [[Josh McDowell]]. Philosopher [[Peter Kreeft]] describes the trilemma as "the most important argument in Christian apologetics",<ref>Kreeft, Peter (1988). [http://www.peterkreeft.com/topics/christ-divinity.htm "The Divinity of Christ"]. ''Fundamentals of the Faith: Essays in Christian Apologetics''. San Francisco: [[Ignatius Press]]. p. 59. {{ISBN|0-89870-202-X}}. Retrieved 13 April 2007.</ref> and it forms a major part of the first talk in the [[Alpha Course]] and the book based on it, ''Questions of Life'' by [[Nicky Gumbel]], an English Anglican priest. [[Ronald Reagan]] used this argument in 1978, in a written reply to a liberal Methodist minister who said that he did not believe Jesus was the son of God.<ref>Von Damm, Helene, ed. (1980). ''Sincerely, Ronald Reagan''. New York: Berkley. p. 90.</ref> A variant has also been quoted by [[Bono]].<ref>Michka Assayas, ''Bono in Conversation'', (Riverhead Hardcover, 2005) page 205.</ref> The Lewis version was cited by [[Charles Colson]] as the basis of his conversion to Christianity.<ref>Aitken, Jonathan (2005). ''Charles Colson''. Continuum International. pp. 210–211.</ref> [[Stephen T. Davis|Stephen Davis]], a supporter of Lewis and of this argument,<ref>Davis, Stephen T. (2006). "Was Jesus Mad, Bad, or God?". ''Christian Philosophical Theology''. Oxford University Press. Abstract, Chapter 9, pp. 149f. "In this chapter, C. S. Lewis'[s] famous trilemma argument in favor of the divinity of Christ (Jesus was either mad, bad, or God) is developed, and a version of it is defended."</ref> argues that it can show belief in the [[Incarnation (Christianity)|incarnation]] as rational.<ref>Davis, Stephen T. (2006). ''Christian Philosophical Theology''. Oxford University Press. p. 150. "I ... claim that the MBG argument, properly understood, can establish the rationality of belief in the incarnation of Jesus."</ref> The biblical scholar [[Bruce M. Metzger]] argued: "It has often been pointed out that Jesus' claim to be the only Son of God is either true or false. If it is false, he either knew the claim was false or he did not know that it was false. In the former case (2) he was a liar; in the latter case (3) he was a lunatic. No other conclusion beside these three is possible."<ref>Metzger, Bruce M. (2003) [1964). ''The New Testament: Its Background, Growth, and Content'' (revised ed.). Abingdon. p. 157. {{ISBN|978-0-227-17025-0}}.</ref>

===Non-Christian===
The atheist writer [[Christopher Hitchens]] accepts Lewis's analysis of the options but reaches the opposite conclusion that Jesus was not good. He writes: "I am bound to say that Lewis is more honest here. Absent a direct line to the Almighty and a conviction that the last days are upon us, how is it 'moral' ... to claim a monopoly on access to heaven, or to threaten waverers with everlasting fire, let alone to condemn fig trees and persuade devils to infest the bodies of pigs? Such a person if not divine would be a sorcerer and a fanatic."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/11/books/review/Hitchens-t.html |title=In the Name of the Father, the Sons... |last=Hitchens |first=Christopher |work=The New York Times |date=9 July 2010 |issn=0362-4331|access-date=10 February 2015}}</ref>

==Criticism==
Writing of the argument's "almost total absence from discussions about the status of Jesus by professional theologians and biblical scholars",<ref>Davis, Stephen T. (2006). ''Christian Philosophical Theology''. Oxford University Press. p. 151</ref> [[Stephen T. Davis]] comments that it is "often severely criticized, both by people who do and by people who do not believe in the divinity of Jesus".<ref name="Davis 2006, p. 150">Davis, Stephen T. (2006). ''Christian Philosophical Theology''. Oxford University Press. p. 150.</ref>

===Jesus' claims to divinity===
The argument relies on the assumption that Jesus claimed to be God,<ref name="lord_jesus_christ_a01">{{cite book | last1 = Hurtado | first1 = Larry W. | title = Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity |url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_MH-_ZQuZrgC&pg=PA5 | year = 2005 | publisher = Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Company | isbn = 0-8028-3167-2 | page = 5 }}</ref> something that most biblical scholars and historians do not believe to be true.<ref name="Hick page 27">{{Bulleted list|{{cite book | last=Hick | first=John | title=The Metaphor of God Incarnate: Christology in a Pluralistic Age | publisher=Presbyterian Publishing Corporation | date=2006 | orig-date=1993 | isbn=978-0-664-23037-1 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f-QMmFx8hwcC&pg=PA27 | access-date=5 January 2024 | page=27 | quote=A further point of broad agreement among New Testament scholars ... is that the historical Jesus did not make the claim to deity that later Christian thought was to make for him: he did not understand himself to be God, or God the Son, incarnate. ... such evidence as there is has led the historians of the period to conclude, with an impressive degree of unanimity, that Jesus did not claim to be God incarnate.}}|{{cite book | first=John | last=Hick | title=Four Views on Salvation in a Pluralistic World | publisher=Zondervan Academic | date=2010 | orig-date=1996, 1995 | isbn=978-0-310-87238-2 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lAJO7vQNrqQC&dq=%2522Jesus+did+not+claim%2522+consensus&pg=PA85 | access-date=16 October 2025 | page=85 | quote=Thus I agree with Douglas Geivett and Gary Phillips that if Jesus did not claim to be God, “then the logical status of the Incarnation is moot, for it presupposes that Jesus did regard himself as God." At this point they are more forthright than their colleagues in this book. It is impossible to discuss the relevant New Testament texts here, but I have already quoted in my chapter a number of leading conservative (not liberal) New Testament scholars who, after examination of the texts, are agreed that Jesus did not claim to be God; and this indeed represents a general consensus today within mainline scholarship, whether Catholic or Protestant, conservative or liberal.}}}}</ref><ref name="p696">Sources for opponents of the thesis, who nevertheless admit that "many scholars" or "most scholars" or "liberal and skeptical scholars typically" posit it:{{Bulleted list|{{cite book | last1=Pitre | first1=Brant | last2=Barron | first2=Robert | title=The Case for Jesus: The Biblical and Historical Evidence for Christ | publisher=PRH Christian Publishing | year=2016 | isbn=978-0-7704-3549-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i9LvCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA192 | access-date=8 March 2025 | page=192 | quote=According to many scholars these days, there is a “fourth option”: Jesus never actually claimed to be God.}}|{{cite book | last=Pitre | first=Brant | title=Jesus the Bridegroom: The Greatest Love Story Ever Told | publisher=PRH Christian Publishing | year=2014 | isbn=978-0-7704-3546-2 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3SnbAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA210 | access-date=8 March 2025 | page=210 | quote=Finally, and most significant of all, I began to realize that many contemporary New Testament scholars do not believe that Jesus of Nazareth ever actually claimed to be God. Of all the ideas that I encountered, this last one shook me to my core.}}|{{cite book | last=Pitre | first=Brant | title=Jesus and Divine Christology | publisher=Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing | year=2024 | isbn=978-1-4674-6857-2 | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tUYbEQAAQBAJ&dq=Ehrman%2527s+assessment+of+the+modern+quest+as+a+whole+is+quite+accurate&pg=PT10 | access-date=13 April 2025 | page=unpaginated | quote=Ehrman's assessment of the modern quest as a whole is quite accurate. | chapter=Chapter 1. The Quest and Jesus's Divinity}}|{{cite book | last=Yoder Neufeld | first=Thomas R. | title=Recovering Jesus: The Witness of the New Testament | publisher=Brazos Press | date=2007 | isbn=978-1-4412-0252-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E4Ji4v7Z9UEC&dq=jesus+claimed+god+%2522most+scholars%2522&pg=PA17 | access-date=1 June 2025 | pages=17–18 | quote=Many (most?) scholars view this}}|{{cite book | last=Cowan | first=S.B. | editor-last=House | editor-first=H. Among other things, I show why the majority of critical scholars for more than a century have argued that Jesus is best understood as an apocalyptic prophet who predicted that the end of the age was soon to arrive, when God would intervene in history and overthrow the forces of evil to bring in his good kingdom. New Testament Witness}}}}Source for a consensus claim from 2024:{{Bulleted list|{{cite web | last=Leonard | first=Hunter | title=The Academic Case for the Divinity of Christ | website=Crisis Magazine | date=19 December 2024 | url=https://crisismagazine.com/opinion/the-academic-case-for-the-divinity-of-christ | access-date=14 February 2026 }}}}</ref> A frequent criticism is that Lewis's trilemma depends on the veracity of the scriptural accounts of Jesus's statements and miracles.<ref>Blomberg, Craig L. (1987). ''The Historical Reliability of the Gospels''. Intervarsity Press. p. xx. "The problem with this argument is that it assumes what is regularly denied, namely, that the gospels give entirely accurate accounts of the actions and claims of Jesus ... This option represents the most common current explanation of the more spectacular deeds and extravagant claims of Jesus in the gospels."</ref> The trilemma rests on the interpretation of New Testament authors' depiction of the [[life of Jesus]]; a widespread objection is that the statements by Jesus recorded in the Gospels are being misinterpreted, and do not constitute claims to divinity.<ref name="Davis 2006, p. 150"/> According to the biblical scholar [[Bart D. Ehrman]], it is historically inaccurate that Jesus called himself God, so Lewis's premise of accepting that very claim is problematic. Ehrman stated that it is a mere legend that the [[historical Jesus]] called himself God, and that this was unknown to Lewis since he never was a professional Bible scholar.<ref name="The Bart Ehrman Blog 2013">{{cite web | title=The Problem with Liar, Lunatic, or Lord | website=The Bart Ehrman Blog | date=17 January 2013 | url=https://ehrmanblog.org/the-problem-with-liar-lunatic-or-lord-for-members/ | access-date=23 November 2020}}</ref><ref name="NPR 2014">{{cite web | title=If Jesus Never Called Himself God, How Did He Become One? | website=NPR | date=7 April 2014 | url=https://www.npr.org/2014/04/07/300246095/if-jesus-never-called-himself-god-how-did-he-become-one | access-date=23 November 2020}}</ref>

In ''[[Honest to God]]'', [[John A. T. Robinson]], then [[Bishop of Woolwich]], criticizes Lewis's approach, questioning the idea that Jesus intended to claim divinity: "It is, indeed, an open question whether Jesus claimed to be Son of God, let alone God".<ref>Robinson, John A. T. (1963). ''Honest to God''. London: SCM Press. p. 72.</ref> [[John Hick]], writing in 1993, argued that this "once popular form of apologetic" was ruled out by changes in New Testament studies, citing "broad agreement" that scholars do not today support the view that Jesus claimed to be God, quoting as examples [[Michael Ramsey]] (1980), [[C. F. D. Moule]] (1977), [[James Dunn (theologian)|James Dunn]] (1980), Brian Hebblethwaite (1985), and David Brown (1985).<ref name="Hick page 27"/> [[Larry Hurtado]], who argues that the followers of Jesus within a very short period developed an exceedingly high level of devotional reverence to Jesus, at the same time says that there is no evidence that Jesus himself demanded or received such cultic reverence.<ref name="lord_jesus_christ_a01"/><ref>{{cite web|last=Hurtado|first=Larry|url=https://larryhurtado.wordpress.com/2017/10/09/the-origin-of-divine-christology|title=The Origin of 'Divine Christology'?|website=Larry Hurtado's Blog|date=9 October 2017|access-date=9 May 2024}}</ref> According to [[Gerd Lüdemann]], the broad consensus among modern New Testament scholars is that the proclamation of the divinity of Jesus was a development within the earliest Christian communities.<ref name=gerd>{{cite journal|author-link=Gerd Lüdemann|last=Lüdemann|first=Gerd|date=October–November 2007|url=http://wwwuser.gwdg.de/~gluedem/download/pope_review.pdf|title=An Embarrassing Misrepresentation|journal=Free Inquiry|access-date=10 May 2024|quote=... the broad consensus of modern New Testament scholars that the proclamation of Jesus's exalted nature was in large measure the creation of the earliest Christian communities.}}</ref>

Donald S. Williams wrote "It is unfair to take a paragraph aimed at a lay audience and complain that it is inadequate to deal with people who have a more sophisticated set of issues."<ref name="t713">{{cite book | first=Donald S. | last=Williams | editor-last=Bassham | editor-first=Gregory | title=C. S. Lewis's Christian Apologetics: Pro and Con | publisher=BRILL | date=2015 | isbn=978-90-04-30165-8 | chapter=Thirteen PRO: A DEFENSE OF C. S. LEWIS’S “TRILEMMA” | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Tg95CgAAQBAJ&dq=Some+of+the++sharpest+critiques,+in+fact,+have+come+from+within+the+believing+community.&pg=PA171 | access-date=2026-02-19 | page=188}}</ref> Williams considers it accomplished apologetics due to the mere fact that it stirs debates.<ref name="t713"/> Williams rejects the consensus of mainstream Bible scholars as irrelevant for conservative believers.{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=178}} Hence, the apologetic argument is valid, since it convinces conservative Christians.{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=178}} Williams argues that, taking the Bible at face value, Jesus did claim to be God.{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=178}} Williams thinks that scholars who do not take the Bible at face value are [[Methodological naturalism|naturalistic skeptics]].{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=178}} Williams stated "Lewis did not present the Trilemma as a proof of the deity of Christ as such",{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=204}} i.e. Lewis just clarified the options.{{sfn|Williams|2015|p=172}}

===Unsound logical form===
Another criticism raised is that Lewis is creating a [[false trilemma]] by insisting that only three options are possible. [[Craig A. Evans]] writes that the "liar, lunatic, Lord" trilemma "makes for good alliteration, maybe even good rhetoric, but it is faulty logic". He proceeds to list several other alternatives: Jesus was [[Israel's messiah]], simply a great prophet, or we do not really know who or what he was because the New Testament sources portray him inaccurately.<ref>Evans, Craig Alan (2007). "Misplaced Faith and Misguided Suspicions". ''Fabricating Jesus: How Modern Scholars Distort the Gospels''. IVP Books. pp. 20–21.</ref> Philosopher and theologian [[William Lane Craig]] has also criticized the argument for its incompleteness, suggesting “legend” as a fourth alternative that could be added and excluded.<ref>Craig, William Lane (1994). ''Reasonable Faith: Christian Truth and Apologetics''. Crossway Books. pp. 38–39.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Correcting Wikipedia {{!}} Reasonable Faith |url=https://www.reasonablefaith.org/writings/question-answer/correcting-wikipedia |access-date=2025-10-01 |website=www.reasonablefaith.org |language=en}}</ref> Philosopher John Beversluis comments that Lewis "deprives his readers of numerous alternate interpretations of Jesus that carry with them no such odious implications".<ref>Beversluis, John (1985). ''C. S. Lewis and the Search for Rational Religion''. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans. p. 56.</ref> [[Paul E. Little]], in his 1967 work ''[[Know Why You Believe]]'', expanded the argument into a [[tetralemma]] ("Lord, Liar, Lunatic or Legend"). This has also been done by [[Peter Kreeft]] and Ronald Tacelli, both [[Saint John's Seminary (Massachusetts)|Saint John's Seminary]] professors of philosophy at [[Boston College]], who have also suggested a pentalemma, accommodating the option that Jesus was a [[guru]], who believed himself to be God in the sense that everything is divine.<ref>Kreeft, Peter; Tacelli, Ronald (1994). ''Handbook of Christian Apologetics''. Madison. pp. 161–174.</ref>

====Lewis's response to the possibility that the Gospels are legends====
Lewis used his own literary expertise in a 1950 essay, "What Are We to Make of Jesus?", to disagree with the possibility that the Gospels are legends. There, Lewis writes:

<blockquote>"Now, as a literary historian, I am perfectly convinced that whatever else the Gospels are they are not legends. I have read a great deal of legend and I am quite clear that they are not the same sort of thing. They are not artistic enough to be legends. From an imaginative point of view they are clumsy, they don't work up to things properly. Most of the life of Jesus is totally unknown to us, as is the life of anyone else who lived at that time, and no people building up a legend would allow that to be so. Apart from bits of the Platonic dialogues, there is no conversation that I know of in ancient literature like the Fourth Gospel. There is nothing, even in modern literature, until about a hundred years ago when the realistic novel came into existence."<ref>{{cite web |last=Taylor |first=Justin |date=1 February 2016 |title=Is C.S. Lewis's Liar-Lord-or-Lunatic Argument Unsound? |url=https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/is-c-s-lewiss-liar-lord-or-lunatic-argument-unsound/ |access-date=12 March 2023 |website=The Gospel Coalition}}</ref></blockquote>

===Apologetic method===
Writing from a [[Presuppositional apologetics|presuppositional]] perspective, [[Richard L. Pratt Jr.]] has criticized the trilemma as expanded by [[Paul E. Little]] ("Lord, Liar, Lunatic or Legend") as being too reliant on human reason: "Instead of insisting on the necessity of repentance and faith as the ground for true knowledge, Little acts as if the unbeliever needs merely to be logical about Jesus' claims in order to arrive at the truth."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pratt |first1=Richard L. |author1-link=Richard L. Pratt Jr. |title=Every Thought Captive: A Study Manual for the Defense of Christian Truth |date=1979 |publisher=[[P&R Publishing]] |page=76 |isbn=978-0-87552-352-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XsHC9muwXRsC&pg=PA76 |access-date=1 November 2024}}</ref>
